title: Lobbying

definition.text: Lobbying is legal advocacy that tries to influence decisions made by legislators, regulators or sometimes judges.

facts.text: Its main form is meeting lawmakers directly, armed with research, data and draft proposals.
Lobbyists can be individuals, corporations, nonprofits, interest groups and political action committees.
Inside lobbying deals with decision-makers directly; outside lobbying pressures them by mobilising public opinion.
Research documents three effects: trading money for access, persuading officials with information, and mobilising citizens or coalitions.
Lobbying can pull politicians away from the median voter, especially when special-interest money is high and public attention low.
It can encourage lax enforcement of laws and is seen as one cause of a democratic deficit.
Many governments require lobbyists to register and disclose spending, clients and issues.
A 2011 study found that firms spending most on lobbying relative to assets earned 'blistering' returns.

contested_note: The ethics of lobbying are disputed: it is defended as legitimate advocacy and attacked as corrupting the law for private interests.

definition.text: The fossil fuels lobby is the paid representatives of oil, gas and coal companies and related industries such as chemicals, plastics and aviation.

facts.text: Their wealth and economic importance give them the means to seek outsized influence on government policy.
The lobby promotes climate change denial and obstructs environmental and climate policy.
Lobbyists work to keep fossil fuel subsidies.
Fossil fuel interests spent $2 billion on climate-change lobbying in the US from 2000 to 2016, many times what citizens and environmentalists spent.
The five biggest oil and gas companies spent at least 251 million euros lobbying the EU on climate policy since 2010.
According to the UNFCCC, 636 fossil fuel lobbyists attended COP27.
In Canada, fossil fuel lobbyists contacted officials five times more than environmental groups between 2011 and 2018.
The lobby has used crises such as COVID-19 and the 2022 invasion of Ukraine to try to roll back regulations.
